title: Rate equations
examples: How do I find the rate law if I only have concentration data?
What is the difference between the overall order and the molecularity?
Can I use the initial rates method to find the rate constant?

explain.say: Today we are looking at how fast reactions happen.
The rate law shows the mathematical relationship between concentrations and the reaction rate.
The exponents m and n are the reaction orders with respect to A and B.
The rate constant k has units that depend on the overall reaction order.

items: First order: units are inverse time
Second order: units are inverse concentration/time

draw.text: Units of k: depend on order

explain.say: We use initial rates data to determine the unknown reaction orders m and n.
In a real lab, measuring initial rates helps us find the rate law.

faq.q: How do I know if the reaction is first order or second order?
faq.a: You must use the initial rates method or plot a graph to determine the order. The data itself will guide you to the correct mathematical relationship.
asks: What method tells me the order?
How do I figure out the reaction order?

faq.q: Does the rate constant k change with temperature?
faq.a: Yes, the rate constant k is highly dependent on temperature. Increasing the temperature generally increases the value of k.
asks: Is k constant at different temperatures?

faq.q: What does the overall reaction order mean?
faq.a: The overall reaction order is the sum of the individual orders m plus n. It tells us how the rate depends on all reactants combined.
asks: How do I find the overall order?

faq.q: Should I use the integrated rate law if I have initial rates data?
faq.a: No, if you are using initial rates data, you should use the method of initial rates to find the orders first. The integrated rate law is used later for concentration vs time plots.
asks: When do I use the integrated rate law?
Do I need to calculate k using the integrated form?

faq.q: Is the rate law the same as the stoichiometry?
faq.a: No, the rate law is not always the same as the balanced chemical equation. The exponents in the rate law are determined experimentally, not just by the coefficients.
asks: Are the coefficients the same as the orders?
Does stoichiometry determine the rate law?

facts: The rate law is determined experimentally, not from the balanced equation.
The rate constant k is constant for a specific reaction at a fixed temperature.
The overall order is the sum of the individual orders for each reactant.
Initial rates data is used to find the reaction orders m and n.

quiz.say: If doubling the concentration of reactant A quadruples the rate, what is the order with respect to A?
quiz.why: If the rate quadruples when concentration doubles, the relationship must be proportional to the square, so the order is two.

wrong.1: This would mean the rate doubles when the concentration doubles, which is incorrect for the given data.
wrong.2: This would mean the rate increases by a factor of eight when the concentration doubles, which is too high.
wrong.3: This would mean the rate does not change at all, which contradicts the problem statement.

quiz.say: For a reaction $A + 2B \rightarrow Products$, if the rate law is found to be Rate = k[A][B]^2, what is the overall reaction order?
quiz.why: The overall order is the sum of the individual orders, one from A and two from B, resulting in three.

wrong.0: This is mathematically correct but the answer should be the integer value three.
wrong.2: This incorrectly sums the stoichiometric coefficients of A and B.
wrong.3: This only considers the order with respect to A, ignoring B.

quiz.say: If the rate law is Rate = k[A]^1[B]^1, and you double [A] and halve [B], what is the new rate relative to the original rate?
quiz.why: Doubling [A] multiplies the rate by two, and halving [B] multiplies the rate by one half. Two times one half equals one.

wrong.0: This only accounts for the change in [B] and ignores the change in [A].
wrong.1: This only accounts for the change in [A] and ignores the change in [B].
wrong.2: This incorrectly adds the factors of change together.
